- If sentiment is strongly bullish (≥0.67) in recent days, model tends to overestimate and should be capped or adjusted downward by 1–2% to avoid overshoot.
- If sentiment is bearish (≤0.33) and price is rising, model often underestimates — increase forecast slightly to reflect momentum.
- After sharp spikes (e.g., >5% from prior day), model frequently overreacts and forecasts continued steep rise — reduce forecast slope or add mean-reversion term.
- When sentiment is mixed or neutral (0.33–0.67), model often fails to capture volatility — add ±1–2% buffer around median forecast for uncertainty.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 days after peak) and model continues upward, reduce forecast by 0.5–1.5% per day until reversion completes.
- For 30-day horizon, model often underestimates tail risk — add 1–3% upward adjustment if sentiment is neutral or slightly bullish.
- If sentiment is consistently negative and price is falling, model may underestimate the drop — adjust downward by 0.5–1.5% per day to reflect sentiment-driven sell-off.
